questions.title: Student 1 · Area model for 42 × 13
questions.hint: Check whether the sides of the box add up to 42 and 13.
steps: Look at the top: 40 + 2 = 42. Look at the side: 10 + 3 = 13.
Every part of 42 is multiplied by every part of 13, so the plan works. Mark Yes and explain why.
questions.answer: Yes. Student 1 splits 42 into 40 + 2 and 13 into 10 + 3 and finds all four partial products (400, 20, 120 and 6). Adding them would give the product.

questions.title: Student 2 · (40 × 20) + (2 × 3)
questions.hint: Does 13 have a 20 in it?
steps: Break 13 into tens and ones: 13 = 10 + 3, not 20 + 3.
Notice that the parts 40 × 3 and 2 × 10 are missing too.
Since the numbers and the parts are wrong, mark No and explain.
questions.answer: No. 13 is 10 + 3, so there is no 20 to multiply by, and the plan leaves out partial products such as 40 × 3 and 2 × 10. (It would give 806, not 546.)
questions.verification: Computed (40×20)+(2×3) = 806 ≠ 42×13 = 546 in Python; checked that 13 = 10 + 3.

questions.title: Student 3 · 13 × 40 + 13 × 2
questions.hint: Is 40 + 2 the same as 42?
steps: Adding the two parts gives 13 × 42, which equals 42 × 13. Mark Yes and explain.
questions.answer: Yes. Student 3 breaks 42 into 40 + 2 and multiplies each part by 13. Because 13 × 42 = 42 × 13, adding the two parts gives the product.
questions.verification: Computed 13×40 + 13×2 = 520 + 26 = 546 = 42×13 in Python; order of factors does not change the product.

questions.title: Be Curious · How are they the same?
questions.hint: Compare the final answers and count the rows of work.
steps: Look at the bottom number of each problem.
Count how many partial products each one writes.
Tell one way they are the same and one way they are different.
questions.answer: One possible answer: Both multiply 443 × 15 and get 6,645. The left one writes six small partial products (2,000, 200, 15, 4,000, 400, 30); the right one uses regrouping to write only two partial products (2,215 and 4,430).

questions.title: Math is… Generalizations · two 3-digit numbers
questions.hint: How many digits does the bottom number have?
steps: A 2-digit factor gives 2 partial products (ones and tens).
A 3-digit factor has ones, tens and hundreds.
So you would find 3 partial products and add them.
questions.answer: Sample answer: With two 3-digit numbers you multiply by the ones, the tens and the hundreds, so there are three partial products to add instead of two.
questions.verification: Reasoned from the algorithm; checked example 549×126 = 3,294 + 10,980 + 54,900 = 69,174 in Python.

questions.title: 14 · Extend Your Thinking
questions.hint: Look for the partial products hiding inside the algorithm.
steps: Remember that partial products split a factor into ones and tens.
In the algorithm, each row is a combined partial product.
Explain how knowing one helps you understand the other.
questions.answer: Sample answer: The algorithm uses the same partial products, just combined. When I multiply by the ones digit and then the tens digit, I am finding the same pieces as with partial products, so I understand why each row and each zero is there.
questions.verification: Concept explanation checked against the page's Learn example (549×26 = 3,294 + 10,980).

questions.title: Reflect · Algorithm vs. partial products
questions.hint: Count how many rows each method needs.
steps: Think about how many partial products you write with each method.
Explain why fewer rows can save time.
questions.answer: Sample answer: An algorithm combines several small partial products into one row by regrouping, so there are fewer numbers to write and add. For 443 × 15 it uses 2 rows instead of 6.
questions.verification: Compared the two methods on page 169: 443×15 = 6,645 both ways in Python.
